problem: The chapter defines pitch as the linear distance travelled in one revolution. Standard textbooks define pitch as the axial distance between corresponding points on adjacent threads; the distance travelled in one revolution is the lead (lead = pitch × number of starts). The numbers are right only because a single-start screw is assumed, but a student can carry the wrong definition to a multi-start screw.
fix: Define both: pitch p is the axial distance between adjacent threads (mm); lead L is the distance travelled in one revolution (mm/rev), and L = p for a single-start screw. Then write v = f L / N with L in mm/rev, and note L = p only for single-start.

problem: The speed formula n = f/N and v = f p/N is used without saying that N must be the steps per revolution of the drive mode actually used. In half-step mode a 1.8° motor has 400 steps per revolution, so using N = 200 with the same pulse rate gives double the true speed. A student can lose marks here.
fix: Add one line: use N for the mode in use — 200 for full step, 400 for half step, and the commanded microsteps per revolution for microstepping. The step angle 360°/N then refers only to the full-step value.

problem: "At low speed the available torque exceeds pull-in torque, so it starts" compares the motor's own torque with a torque limit. Pull-in torque is the load limit at that pulse rate; the correct comparison is between the load torque and the pull-in torque. As written, the answer can be reproduced by students as a wrong statement.
fix: "At low speed the pull-in torque of the motor is larger than the load torque, so the rotor starts and keeps step. As the pulse rate rises, winding inductance limits current build-up and the pull-in torque falls. A fast ramp asks for acceleration torque on top of load torque, the total can exceed the pull-in torque at that rate, and the rotor slips or stalls."
